newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Sept 13.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- UK FACES FIGHT ON BSE CULL

British agriculture minister Douglas Hogg is to meet his European Commission counterpart Franz Fischler next week to discuss British plans to abandon the planned cull of 125,000 cattle most at risk of contracting BSE. The abandonment of the cull was the main topic of discussion at the first cabinet meeting since the summer holiday, and Britain's plans -- made in the light of new research suggesting that BSE will die out naturally without a cull -- will put the country on a collision course with the EU.
-- BTR AIMS TO SHED 37 BUSINESSES IN GLOBAL SHAKE-UP

Industrial conglomerate BTR has announced a global restructuring programme, including the disposal of 37 businesses, which will require the group to take charges of 622 million stg. The group, which announced nominal first-half profits of 4 million stg on turnover of 4.95 billion stg, says it intends to shed low-growth businesses to enhance its capacity to expand its core engineering and manufacturing operations.
-- GERMANY BLOCKS BAe MOVE FOR DEFENCE COMPANY

The German defence ministry has scuppered plans by BAe to form an Anglo-German consortium to bid for the German defence electronics company STN Atlas after indicating it wants the company to go to a domestic buyer. STN Atlas is one of the profitable units within the bankrupt Bremer Vulcan group, and BAe had hoped to join with Daimler-Benz Aerospace in the bidding.
-- EU CLOSE TO DEAL OVER ENFORCING STABILITY IN EMU

The European Union is close to agreement on two initiatives designed to stabilise economic and monetary union (Emu) planned for 1999. It expects to receive consent this month for a plan to impose sanctions on member countries of a single currency if they run up excessive deficits. And finance ministers and central bankers are reported to be close to agreement on a remodelled exchange rate mechanism, which will manage currency relations between EU and non-EU countries.
-- INFLATION STAYS ABOVE CLARKE'S 2.5 PER CENT TARGET

The underlying rate of inflation remained at 2.8 percent for the fourth consecutive month in August, denting the hopes of Chancellor Kenneth Clarke of approaching the next general election with low price growth. Clarke has pledged to bring the underlying rate down to 2.5 per cent. Some commentators still expect that target to be achieved, as supermarkets prepare for an expected price war this autumn to go with the current reductions in telephone tariffs.
-- NEW BZW CHIEF ORDERS RESHUFFLE OF SENIOR MANAGERS

Bill Harrison, the new chief executive of Barclays Bank investment arm BZW, has announced a wide-ranging management reshuffle as the bank gears up to challenge US rivals and Swiss and German investment banking arms on a global scale. BZW acting chief executive Donald Brydon is to leave following the recruitment of Bob Diamond, former head of bond trading and sales at CS First Boston in New York.
-- TUC URGES RIGHTS PACKAGE ON BLAIR

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) meeting in Blackpool has further embarrassed Labour leader Tony Blair after calling for a package of worker rights which goes much further than Blair is prepared to accept. The package, which the TUC wants a future Labour government to introduce, includes legal rights of employment for all workers (including part time, temporary and contract), the banning of 'zero-hour' contracts, and the right of workers to take sympathetic industrial action.
-- ELECTRONICS GRANT SEEN AS 'UNFAIR'

Rival electronics companies have protested at the awarding of government grants totalling 23.5 million stg to circuit board maker Interconnection Systems (ISL). The grants were awarded in July to entice the firm to locate a 120 million stg factory in Tyneside, northeast England. But industry trade association the Printed Circuits Interconnection Federation has channelled numerous complaints from smaller firms that the grants will create unfair competition and threaten jobs at other companies.
-- BRITISH GAS CLOSES IN ON CONTRACTS

British Gas has said that it hopes to clinch renegotiation soon over some of its punitive 'take-or-pay' gas contracts with North Sea producers. British Gas is locked into 40 billion stg- worth of long-term contracts requiring it to pay North Sea producers for gas at a set rate -- well above current market prices -- even if it has no use for the gas. But the group hopes that if a handful of producers agree to a deal, then others will follow suit.
-- STRONG DEMAND HELPS LOGICA TO 22 PERCENT RISE

UK-based computer services group Logica has reported a 22 percent increase in full-year pre-tax profits, to 24.7 million stg. With strong demand for information technology, turnover grew 14 percent to 284.8 million stg. Expansion in continental Europe, including a number of start-up operations, saw revenues from continental Europe grow 35 percent, to 61.5 million stg.
